# A Text Analysis Pipeline

Build a pipeline that turns free text (incident report descriptions, or the
field notes on an observation) into tokens, counts terms, and scores documents
with TF-IDF so the terms that distinguish one report from another stand out. A
distinct kind of analysis: text mining.

-   Tokenization turns free text into countable units.
-   Term frequency is a start; TF-IDF down-weights terms that appear everywhere.
-   A document becomes a vector of term weights, so text can be compared like numbers.
-   Text needs the same cleaning and validation as numeric data.

## From text to tokens

-   Incident reports arrive as free text, not as rows and columns, so the first
    job is to turn each report into units we can count.
-   A token is one countable unit, here a single whitespace-separated word.
-   The ecology twin is the same shape: field notes stand in for report
    descriptions and run through the same code.
-   Our tokenizer does three things: lowercase, strip punctuation, and split on
    whitespace.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=imports >}}

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=tokenize >}}

-   Lowercasing turns "Flood" and "flood" into the same token, which is what we
    want when we count.
-   `str.translate` with `str.maketrans("", "", string.punctuation)` removes
    punctuation in one pass.
-   Splitting on whitespace is the simplest possible tokenizer; a real pipeline
    would also handle contractions, numbers, and domain jargon.

## Count terms

-   The simplest summary of a document is how often each term appears, its term
    frequency.
-   `collections.Counter` turns a list of tokens into counts in one call.
-   Divide each count by the number of tokens so a longer document does not
    automatically score higher.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=term_frequency >}}

-   d2 and d4 have four tokens, so their frequencies are 0.25 instead of a
    third; normalizing by length keeps the comparison fair.

## Down-weight common terms

-   Term frequency is a start, but "flood" appears in three of five reports and
    tells us little about any single one.
-   Document frequency counts how many documents contain a term.
-   Inverse document frequency (IDF) is high for rare terms and low for common
    ones: it is the log of total documents over document frequency.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=document_frequency >}}

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=idf_weights >}}

-   A term that appears in every document has document frequency equal to the
    total, so its IDF is log(1), which is zero.
-   Terms unique to one document get the highest IDF, about 1.609 here.

## TF-IDF

-   TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by inverse document frequency.
-   A term scores high only if it is frequent in this document and rare in the
    others, which is exactly what distinguishes one report from the rest.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=tfidf >}}

## Documents as vectors

-   A document is now a vector of term weights, one dimension per term.
-   Most entries are zero because most terms do not appear in most documents.
-   Gather the weights into a tidy Polars frame, one row per document-term pair,
    then pivot into a document-by-term matrix.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=vectors >}}

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=matrix >}}

-   Pivot spreads the `term` column into one column per term, and
    `fill_null(0.0)` records the terms absent from a document as zero.
-   The top-weighted term in each document is the one that separates it from the
    others.

{{< inc text-analysis/text-analysis.py mark=top_terms >}}

-   Each document's top term appears in that document alone, which is why its
    IDF, and therefore its TF-IDF, is high.
-   Text needs the same cleaning as numbers: lowercase before comparing, strip
    punctuation, and decide what to do about typos and near-duplicates.
-   The ecology twin swaps incident descriptions for field notes and runs the
    same pipeline unchanged.
-   A real pipeline would next remove stopwords and stem words; the standard
    library gives us the counting pieces, and we assemble the rest ourselves.
